CausalChain: DDR gene alterations -> Accumulation of DNA damage and cytosolic DNA fragments -> Activation of cGAS-STING pathway -> Production of type I interferons (promoting immune activation) -> However, high TGF-β levels in the BTC tumor microenvironment suppress interferon signaling and T-cell infiltration -> Inhibition of TGF-β removes this suppression -> Combined DDR modulation and TGF-β blockade leads to enhanced T cell mediated antitumor response -> Improved efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Hypothesis: In biliary tract cancer, co-targeting DDR pathways (to boost innate immune activation via the cGAS-STING pathway) and TGF-β signaling (to alleviate immunosuppression) will convert the tumor microenvironment from ‘cold’ to ‘hot’ and synergistically enhance the response to immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTC) remain largely refractory to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), despite the presence of biomarkers such as PD‐L1, tumor mutational burden (TMB), and DNA damage repair (DDR) gene alterations that in other tumors predict response. A key challenge in BTC is the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), which may counter the immunogenic effects of DDR dysfunction and neoantigen generation. We hypothesize that the simultaneous targeting of DDR-induced innate immune activation and the TGF-β mediated immunosuppressive milieu can convert the ‘cold’ BTC microenvironment into an inflamed, ‘hot’ state, thereby sensitizing tumors to ICIs. Our strategy would combine DDR modulators (such as PARP inhibitors) to heighten cytosolic DNA and activate the cGAS-STING pathway with TGF-β inhibitors to relieve stromal suppression, ultimately enhancing type I interferon responses and T cell infiltration. This dual-targeting approach may open a novel therapeutic avenue for overcoming resistance in BTC to immunotherapy.
